To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a peptide antagonist to the dimerization of the HIV-1 accessory factor Vif blocks viral infectivity in nonpermissive cells by preventing Vif from excluding hA3G from viral particles.
a peptide antagonist that blocks the dimerization of the HIV-1 Vif protein inhibits viral replication in non-permissive cells by increasing the incorporation of hA3G into viral particles.

We have shown that Vif multimer formation is a prerequisite for the exclusion of the host defence factor hA3G from virion particles during their assembly and that blocking Vif multimerisation is an effective strategy to sustain the anti-viral activity of hA3G in HIV-1-infected cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel antiretrovirus therapeutics based on the inhibition of Vif multimers.
the development of antiretrovials for the treatment of HIV/AIDS.
the mechanism by which HIV-1 Vif protein blocks antiviral activity of human APOB3G.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we demonstrate that a Vif multimer antagonist blocks Vif dimer formation, which in turn leads to an accumulation of hA3G within viral particles.
Vif dimer formation is essential for HIV-1 infectivty in the presence of hA3G and that the mechanism of Vif dimesrization is required to prevent hA3G packaging into virions during viral assembly.
we have developed a new antiviral strategy that targets a critical step in the HIV-1 life cycle, namely the exclusion of APOB3G from viral particles by Vif.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Vif dimerisation is a valid target for antiviral therapy and we have demonstrated that a peptide antagonist can block Vif multimerisation in a cell based assay.
blocking VIF dimerization is a novel approach to HIV/AIDS treatment.
